name: Kira Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. So you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer for fresh and chilled food at Greenfield Foods, a wholesaler that supplies restaurants and small shops. My day starts at 6, when I check overnight prices from the produce markets and call two or three growers. Then I set the day's order, argue about a late truck, and spend the afternoon on forecasts for the weekend. I love the growers and the speed, but the 5 a.m. alarms and the constant spoilage maths wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does your life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and live with my partner Tomas, who's a physiotherapy assistant, in a rented flat near the ring road. We split everything, and we've got under a month of savings between us. The pay for a senior buyer here is lower than people think, and there's hardly another wholesaler in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected: a bit of help, no revolution. At work I'd tell my boss Dalia that our forecasting tool is fine and we should keep using it. With friends I'd shrug, because the weather moves my numbers far more than any program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd say it keeps me comfortable but never safe. The routine part of my day, matching invoices and updating price sheets, might shrink by an hour. That's fine, but our margins are thin, and a bad month could make Greenfield trim hours anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the forecast helper I already have. I'd save a bit more each month, maybe 150, so Tomas and I get to one month in the bank. If the extra hour appears, I'd spend it visiting growers, since that's where the best prices come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, a little boring, and that's fine. I still feel the rent each month, though, so I'm not exactly relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. What do you use it for today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said the weather matters more than the program. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first sign of trouble look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last July a heatwave wiped out the lettuce for a week. No tool saw it coming, but a grower called Marek (a supplier of ours) had warned me. I switched to a farm two valleys over and saved us about 6,000 in missed orders.

say: I'd say **no revolution**, and our forecasting tool is fine as it is.
I'd tell friends the **weather** moves my numbers more than any program.
think: I'm comfortable but not safe, because thin margins could cut **Greenfield's hours** anyway.
Matching invoices and price sheets might shrink by an **hour a day**.
do: Keep using the **forecast helper** I already have.
Save **150 a month** so Tomas and I reach one month in the bank.
Spend any spare hour **visiting growers** for better prices.
feel: **Steady** and a little bored, but the rent still presses.
S0.quote: Last July a heatwave wiped out the lettuce for a week. No tool saw it coming, but a grower called Marek (a supplier of ours) had warned me.
fieldNote: Calm about AI, but her **money position** keeps her uneasy.

Uses one tool already, so a mild scenario costs her little.

steps.text: Keep using the forecast helper for weekend orders
Save 150 a month toward one month of expenses
Spend spare time visiting growers to find better prices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and we should be using the tools before our competitors do. At work I'd tell Dalia (my boss) that I'll run a trial on order planning. To friends I'd say the changes are fine as long as the people doing the routine work get a fair move to something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it hits my desk directly. Planning and buying are on that list word for word, and a distributor like Greenfield could do the same orders with two buyers instead of four. I'm the senior one, so I think I'd survive, but I'd be the one deciding who goes, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose a trial where I run the forecasting tool on frozen goods first, and I'd learn it properly, not just use it now and then. I'd put a course on my calendar, maybe two evenings a month. Tomas and I would cut our eating out to once a month and move 200 a month to savings. And I'd make sure Dalia knows I'm the person who can run the new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and heavy at the same time. I like learning, but the pay is low and one bad turn makes us tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those thinking tasks is closest to your own desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd hate being the one who chooses. What would you do?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Dalia and the team handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the junior people to move into supplier relations or quality checks instead of being let go. I'd tell Dalia I'll take the tool training first, so I understand what it can and can't do. If the plan is to cut people, I'd want to hear it from Dalia (my boss) before anybody else.

say: I'd say it's **real**, and we should use the tools before our competitors do.
I'd tell friends that routine workers deserve a **fair move** to other work.
think: Planning and buying are on that list, so my desk is **directly affected**.
Greenfield could run on **two buyers** instead of four, and I'd choose who goes.
do: Run a **trial** of the forecasting tool on frozen goods first.
Take a **course** two evenings a month to learn the tools properly.
Cut eating out and move **200 a month** to savings.
feel: **Excited** and heavy together, because the pay leaves no room for error.
S1.quote: If the plan is to cut people, I'd want to hear it from Dalia (my boss) before anybody else.
fieldNote: Treats change as a **chance**, but the card describes her own tasks.
Fears the moral weight of choosing who stays.
Steady adopter, so moves first on tools and training.

steps.text: Run a trial of the forecasting tool on frozen goods
Take an evening course on planning tools twice a month
Cut eating out to once a month and save 200

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and the people in charge should say so out loud. At work I'd say Greenfield needs a plan for buyers within the year. With friends I'd say the news is good for nobody who's paid to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone in about two years, or it turns into one person watching a machine. Wholesale buying is nearly all thinking work. Tomas (my partner) works with his hands, so his job likely lasts until the robots catch up, about 2031, and that's our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd cut spending down to rent, food and bills and aim for three months saved. I'd start applying to hands-on roles, maybe at a health clinic or a food warehouse floor, since robots come three years later. I'd ask Tomas to keep his hours and look for extra shifts. I'd also see if Dalia would write me a reference now, while Greenfield is still doing well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a train platform when the train's already moving. I'd probably cry once, then make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas works with his hands, kind of. How does his job fit in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd cry once and then make a list. What's on the list?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas the night you read the news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent for four months, what I owe on my master's, Tomas's shifts, and three names of people who might hire me. I'd put 'call Marek' near the top, because he knows every food business in the area. People who know me are my best asset.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready**, and companies should have a plan for buyers within the year.
I'd tell friends this is bad for anyone paid to **think**.
think: My job is gone in about two years, or it shrinks to **one person** watching a machine.
Tomas's hands-on work gives us a **safety net** until about 2031.
do: Cut spending to **rent, food and bills** and aim for three months saved.
Apply for **hands-on roles** at a clinic or a food warehouse.
Ask Tomas to take **extra shifts** and ask Dalia for a reference.
feel: Like standing on a **platform** as the train moves, then making a list.
S2.quote: Tomas (my partner) works with his hands, so his job likely lasts until the robots catch up, about 2031, and that's our safety net.
fieldNote: Reads the card closely: thinking jobs go in **2028**, hands-on work around 2031.
Uses her partner's hands-on work as a buffer, and plans to move that way herself.
Stays practical under shock; a list is her coping tool.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bills and save three months
Apply for hands-on jobs at a clinic or food warehouse
Ask Tomas to take extra shifts at the clinic
Ask Dalia for a reference letter while Greenfield is doing well

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same message, but with more detail. We need training funds and a path for buyers to move into new work. At work I'd say let's run pilots now so we learn how it fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I have a real chance. Five years is enough to retrain if I start now, and robots for hands-on work are still three years after that. I'm worried about the dip, because wholesale doesn't have many other roles nearby, so I might need to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd get certified in a data and planning tool, and I'd start a small side income helping a local grower cooperative with their order sheets. I'd keep saving 200 a month toward a three-month buffer. By year three I'd apply for operations or quality roles in the health sector, because Tomas is already there and knows the managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a bumpy road with a visible turn, not a cliff. I'd be tense and also motivated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You mentioned a side income with the growers. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first year look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a cooperative called Valley Growers (a group of local farms), and they do orders on paper and phone. I could build them a simple order sheet. I could run it for a monthly fee, maybe 300. It's small, but it teaches me what the buyers on the other side of the table need.

say: I'd say we need **training funds** and a path for buyers into new work.
I'd tell colleagues to run **pilots** now so we learn how the tools fail.
think: Five years is enough to **retrain** if I start now.
Wholesale has few other roles nearby, so I might have to **move**.
do: Get certified in a **data and planning tool** in year one.
Start a **side income** running order sheets for a grower cooperative.
Save **200 a month** toward a three-month buffer.
feel: Like a **bumpy road** with a visible turn, tense but motivated.
S3.quote: There's a cooperative called Valley Growers (a group of local farms), and they do orders on paper and phone. I could build them a simple order sheet.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **act first** and build a second income.
Plans around Tomas's contacts in health care.
Anxious because the local job market is so thin.

steps.text: Get certified in a data and planning tool this year
Build and run an order sheet for Valley Growers for a monthly fee
Save 200 a month toward a three-month buffer
Apply for operations roles in the health sector by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's long enough to do it well, as long as people don't wait. At work I'd say we should write the new job descriptions now, not when the budget is cut. To friends I'd say learn one new skill a year and don't count on a company to do it for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a gift and a risk. The gift is time to build savings and a second career. The risk is that ten years makes everyone relaxed, and then the lights go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time master's module in data or operations, one a year, paid for partly by Greenfield if I can ask for it. I'd get my savings to six months in about three years. I'd use the AI tools at work every day, so I'm the person on the team who understands them. And Tomas and I would think about buying a small flat in five years, with a smaller place if need be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, even hopeful. The money pressure's still there today, but a long runway makes it feel like a plan, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with a full decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said ten years can make everyone relaxed. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret not doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a yearly check on the calendar, like a car service. Each January I'd ask myself what skill I've picked up. I'd also ask what changed at Greenfield and what the tools can do now.

say: I'd say write the **new job descriptions** now, not when the budget is cut.
I'd tell friends to learn **one new skill** a year.
think: Ten years is **gift and risk**, because people get relaxed and then it hits.
I should use the time to build **savings** and a second career.
do: Take a **part-time module** in data or operations each year.
Raise my savings to **six months** within three years.
Use AI tools at work **every day** so I understand them best.
feel: **Hopeful**, with money pressure that is easier to carry with a long runway.
S4.quote: I'd put a yearly check on the calendar, like a car service. Each January I'd ask myself what skill I've picked up.
fieldNote: With time, she turns anxiety into a **routine** and a plan.
Wants to be the in-house expert on the tools.
Still short of money today, so unease remains.

steps.text: Take one part-time data or operations module each year
Build savings to six months within three years
Use AI tools at work every day

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. There's no time to retrain, and Tomas and I have almost nothing saved. What would help is a payment while you retrain, a notice from companies before they cut jobs, and managers who say plainly what's coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say don't forget the middle people like me. We have good jobs on paper, but our pay is low and our savings are tiny. If we go first, a lot of small families go with us.

headlineQuote: We have good jobs on paper, but our pay is low and our savings are tiny. If we go first, a lot of small families go with us.
portrait: Kira is a 27-year-old lead buyer of fresh food at a **small wholesaler**, living with her partner Tomas.
She earns less than people expect, has **under a month** saved, and sees few similar jobs in town.
She is pragmatic and open to change when it works, and already uses a **forecast tool**.
She faces the fast AGI worlds with a list, a plan to move to **hands-on work**, and Tomas's job as a cushion.
With time she builds **savings**, a side income and a second career.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her most, with no time to retrain and almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **payment** while retraining, advance notice from companies, and managers who say what's coming.
